1.pericope_label: Now of the things which we have spoken this is the sum: We have such an high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens; A minister of the sanctuary, and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin state the drift and the title. Gill takes the opening words of the scope and drift, the compendium and substance, or the principal of what has been said in the three preceding chapters, which is the priesthood of Christ. On the sanctuary he offers three senses: the heavenly one, so called in allusion to the holy of holies which was its type, and because it is truly a holy place which Christ sanctifies and prepares for his people by his presence and intercession; or the Holy Ones, that is the saints who are set apart by the Father and made holy by the Spirit, to whom Christ is a minister in his prophetic office to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, in his priestly office in offering himself a sacrifice and now interceding in heaven, and in his kingly office in governing and defending them; or holy things, such as the gifts of his Spirit, grace and at last glory, and the presenting of their sacrifices of prayer and praise to God. Calvin explains that, so that readers might know the subject he handles, the writer reminds them that his object is to prove that Christ's priesthood, by which that of the law had been abolished, is spiritual; he proceeds with the same argument, but as he contends with various reasonings he introduced this admonition to keep his readers attentive to what he had in view. Having already shown that Christ is a high priest, he now contends that his priesthood is celestial, from which it follows that by his coming the priesthood established by Moses under the law was made void, for it was earthly. Since Christ suffered in the humble condition of his flesh, and having taken the form of a servant made himself of no reputation in the world, the Apostle reminds us of his ascension, by which was removed not only the reproach of the cross but also of that abject and mean condition which he had assumed together with our flesh; for it is by the power of the Spirit which gloriously appeared in the resurrection and the ascension that the dignity of his priesthood is to be estimated. He reasons thus, that since Christ has ascended to the right hand of God that he might reign gloriously in heaven, he is not the minister of the earthly but of the heavenly sanctuary. On the following words Calvin holds that the word is to be taken as neuter, and that it is better to take holy things as designating the holy duties of the priest, afterwards specified when the offering of gifts and sacrifices is mentioned, than as signifying the sanctuary; Christ is a priest and a minister in sacred things, and a minister in the true tabernacle, having holy things to do which he does not in the shadowy and typical tabernacle but in that which is real and celestial. He notes that in the next chapter the word accompanied by the article means the holiest place and without the article the holy place, so that on that meaning the rendering here ought to be the minister of the holiest, but judges that the context here favours the former sense. He then raises a question: whether the tabernacle built by Moses was a false one, and presumptuously constructed, since there is an implied contrast in the words; and answers that the term used here is not set in opposition to what is false but only to what is typical.

Henry gives a summary recital of what had been said concerning the excellency of Christ's priesthood, showing what we have in Christ, where he now resides, and what sanctuary he is the minister of. We have a high priest, and such a high priest as no other people ever had, no age of the world or of the church ever having produced his like, all others being but types and shadows of him; he is adequately fitted and absolutely sufficient to all the intents and purposes of a high priest, both with respect to the honour of God and the happiness of men, and himself the great honour of all those who have an interest in him. He now resides at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty on high, that is of the glorious God of heaven; there the Mediator is placed, possessed of all authority and power both in heaven and upon earth, which Henry calls the reward of his humiliation. This authority he exercises for the glory of his Father, for his own honour, and for the happiness of all who belong to him, and by his almighty power he will bring every one of them in their own order to the right hand of God in heaven, as members of his mystical body.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson supply the analysis and the philology. Barnes sets out the chapter's place in the argument: the apostle had demonstrated that Christ was to be a priest, and not of the Levitical order but of the order of Melchizedek, which involved a change of the law appointing a priesthood, and that in respect to permanence and happy moral influence the priesthood of Christ far surpassed the Jewish; he now shows that it involved a change in the nature of the covenant between God and his people, stating first the sum or principal point of the whole matter, that the priesthood of Christ was real and permanent while that of the Hebrew economy was typical and destined in its own nature to be temporary. On the sanctuary Barnes explains that the Greek may mean either the sanctuary, denoting the Holy of Holies, or holy things; the word was given to the tabernacle or temple as a holy place, and the plural form used here was given to the most holy place by way of eminence, and the connexion seems to require us to understand it of the most holy place and not of holy things, the idea being that the Lord Jesus has entered into the Holy of Holies in heaven of which that in the tabernacle was an emblem. The true tabernacle is the real tabernacle in heaven of which that among the Hebrews was but the type; the word means properly a booth, hut or tent, and was applied to the tent Moses was directed to build as the place for the worship of God, which as the temple afterwards was regarded as the peculiar abode of God on earth, while the reference here is to heaven as the dwelling place of God. Ellicott prefers the rendering, Now in the things which we are saying this is the chief point, noting that opinion has been much divided as to the meaning of the first Greek word, whether it should be taken as summary or as chief point, each meaning being well supported by the usage of the language; the words joined with it lead him to prefer the second, and when the course of the argument is traced he finds it difficult to believe that the writer could express a summary of his thought in the words which follow. He prefers who sat down to who is set, notes that twice before the words of the psalm have been referred to Jesus without their full significance in regard to the present subject having been brought out, and observes that whereas in the previous chapter the meaning of such a one must be sought in what precedes, here the meaning of such is found in the description which the following words contain. On the sanctuary he says the word rendered minister is very commonly used in the Greek Old Testament for the officiating priest, and that it is difficult to decide on the meaning of the words joined with it, whether they denote holy things or holy place, and if the latter what the distinction is between this holy place and the true tabernacle; the ordinary usage of the Epistle would suggest holy place, and the occurrence of both expressions in the next chapter, where there is no doubt as to the translation, is sufficient to remove hesitation. The sanctuary will therefore probably be the heavenly counterpart of the Holiest Place and the true Tabernacle the counterpart of the sacred Tent of Moses, containing both the Holy Place and the Holiest of all; the Holy of Holies is the place of God's immediate presence and the Tabernacle that of God's appointed service, the latter being expressly mentioned here because special reference is to be made to its typical representation upon earth. The word rendered true, he adds, denotes that which is contrasted with everything shadowy or imperfect. Robertson glosses the opening phrase as in the matter of the things being discussed, and the noun as the neuter of an adjective belonging to the head, the main matter, the pith, which is also used of a sum total or a sum of money. The pronoun rendered such, he says, is both retrospective and prospective, and he finds here a summary of five points of superiority in Jesus as high priest: he is himself a better priest than Aaron, he works in a better sanctuary, he offers a better sacrifice, he is mediator of a better covenant, and his work rests on better promises. On the sanctuary he renders it of the holy places without any distinction between the holy place and the most holy, and takes the true tabernacle as the antitype or archetype of the tabernacle in the wilderness in which Aaron served, the ideal tabernacle in heaven of which the earthly tabernacle was a symbol and which the temple merely copied, so that it is the genuine tabernacle; the verb rendered pitched is an old word for fastening the pegs of a tent, occurring here only in the New Testament.

Clarke and Wesley take the office and the tabernacle. Clarke summarises the chapter as giving the sum or chief articles of what the apostle has spoken concerning the eternal priesthood of Christ, the excellency of the new covenant beyond the old, its nature and perfection stated from the predictions of the prophets, and the abolition of the old by the new. On the title he explains that the Greek means a public minister of the holy things or places, the word being compounded of the words for public and for a work or office, so that it means a person who officiated for the public, in whom and in whose work all the people had a common right; hence our word liturgy, the public work of prayer and praise designed for the people at large. Properly speaking, he says, the Jewish priest was the servant of the public who transacted the business of the people with God, and Jesus Christ is the same kind of public officer, since both as Priest and Mediator he transacts the business of the whole human race with God, performing the holy things in the true tabernacle, heaven, of which the Jewish tabernacle was the type. The tabernacle was the place among the Jews where God dwelt by the symbol of his presence, which could only typify heaven where God dwells in his essential glory and is manifest to angels and glorified saints; and the Jewish tabernacle was man's work though made by God's direction, while the heavens, this true tabernacle, are the work of God alone and infinitely more glorious. Wesley notes that, having finished his description of the type in Melchisedec, the apostle begins to treat directly of the excellency of Christ's priesthood beyond the Levitical; that he sat down having finished his oblation, at the right hand of the Majesty, that is of God; that as a minister he represents his own sacrifice as the high priest did the blood of those sacrifices once a year; that the sanctuary is heaven, typified by the holy of holies; and that the true tabernacle is perhaps his human nature, of which the old tabernacle was a type, fixed for ever by the Lord and not by man as Moses fixed the tabernacle.

Chrysostom and Cyril of Jerusalem take the session and the title. Chrysostom observes that Paul mixes the lowly things with the lofty, ever imitating his Master, so that the lowly become the path to the lofty and through the former we are led to the latter, and when we are amid the great things we learn that the lowly ones were a condescension; this he does here also. After declaring that he offered up himself and showing him to be a High Priest, he says that we have such an High Priest who is set down on the right hand of the throne of the majesty — and yet this, Chrysostom notes, is not the office of a Priest but of him whom the Priest should serve. He is called a minister of the sanctuary, not simply a minister, and of the true Tabernacle which the Lord pitched and not man; and Chrysostom bids the reader see the condescension, recalling that a little before the writer had made a separation, asking whether the angels are not all ministering spirits, and saying that it is not said to them, Sit thou on my right hand, for he that sitteth is not a minister. How is it then that it is here said, a minister, and a minister of the Sanctuary, since he means here the Tabernacle? So, Chrysostom says, he raised up the minds of the believing Jews. Cyril of Jerusalem gathers the testimonies to the Son's sitting at the right hand of the Father: in the Gospel according to Matthew it is written that henceforth ye shall see the Son of Man sitting on the right hand of power; in accordance with which the Apostle Peter writes of the Resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is on the right hand of God, having gone into heaven; and the Apostle Paul, writing to the Romans, says that it is Christ that died, yea rather that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God; charging the Ephesians he speaks of the working of his mighty power which he wrought in Christ when he raised him from the dead and set him at his own right hand; the Colossians he taught that if they be risen with Christ they should seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; and in the Epistle to the Hebrews he says that when he had made purification of sins he sat down.

debates: Whether the opening word means a summary or the chief point. Ellicott states the division and decides for chief point, both because of the phrase joined to it and because the following words are no summary; Robertson agrees, calling it the main matter or the pith; Gill gives both senses without choosing between them.

What Christ is minister of. Barnes and Ellicott both decide for a place, the heavenly counterpart of the Holiest; Calvin decides the opposite way, taking the neuter of the priest's holy duties rather than of the sanctuary; Gill adds a third sense, that it may mean the holy ones, the saints themselves; Robertson refuses the distinction between holy place and most holy altogether; Clarke works instead from the word for minister and its public sense.

What the true tabernacle is. Clarke, Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all take it of heaven or of the ideal sanctuary there; Wesley alone suggests that it may be Christ's human nature, of which the old tabernacle was the type; Calvin, meeting the objection that the word would make Moses's tabernacle false, answers that true is opposed here not to what is false but to what is typical.

How one seated can be called a minister. Chrysostom alone presses the difficulty, recalling that the epistle has already argued that he who sits is not a minister, and resolves it by the writer's habit of mixing lowly things with lofty so that the lowly become a path to the lofty; Cyril of Jerusalem, treating only the session, assembles the apostolic testimonies to it; Calvin makes the ascension the measure of the priesthood's dignity.
outliers: Wesley alone declines to identify the true tabernacle with heaven, offering instead Christ's human nature as the reality of which the old tent was the figure.

Chrysostom alone treats the collocation of sitting and serving as a problem to be solved rather than a description to be expounded, and answers it from the rhetorical method of the epistle as a whole.
themes: the throne of the Majesty in the heavens
which the Lord pitched, and not man

3.pericope_label: For every high priest is ordained to offer gifts and sacrifices: wherefore it is of necessity that this man have somewhat also to offer. For if he were on earth, he should not be a priest, seeing that there are priests that offer gifts according to the law: Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin defend the priesthood and the argument. Gill notes that the Socinians attempt to prove from this verse that Christ was not a priest and did not offer sacrifice on earth, whereas his coming into the world and his appearance in human nature was in the character of a priest and to qualify himself for one; his death was his sacrifice, which was on earth, and he never offered but one sacrifice, going to heaven after he had offered himself, just as the sacrifices under the law were first offered before their blood was carried within. The meaning, Gill says, is either that what it was necessary he should have to offer was on earth, or that if his human nature had been earthly, of men, and come by ordinary generation, he had been only typically a priest at most and no better than the typical ones, indeed needless, and might not have offered, not being of Levi's tribe. On the following verse he explains that the priests themselves were types of Christ, the places they ministered in an exemplar of the heavenly places where Christ is, and the things they ministered shadows of the good things which are by Christ; and the shadows were mere representations, dark, obscure and glimmering, and were fleeting and transitory. Calvin states the Apostle's intention, to show that Christ's priesthood cannot coexist with the Levitical, and the proof: the Law appointed priests to offer sacrifices to God, whence it appears that the priesthood is an empty name without a sacrifice; but Christ had no sacrifice such as was offered under the Law, and it follows that his priesthood is not earthly or carnal but of a more excellent character. The first thing deserving notice, he says, is the teaching that no priest is appointed except to offer gifts, from which it is evident that no favour from God can be obtained for men except through the interposition of a sacrifice; hence, that our prayers may be heard they must be founded on a sacrifice, and the audacity of those who pass by Christ and forget his death and yet rush into the presence of God is altogether pernicious and fatal, since God will never hear us unless he is reconciled, and sacrifice must necessarily precede. On the next verse Calvin argues that as the office of a judge does not exist without laws, so the office of sacrificing must be connected with Christ as a priest; yet he has no earthly or visible sacrifice, and cannot then be a priest on earth. We must always hold, he adds, that when the Apostle speaks of the death of Christ he regards not the external action but the spiritual benefit: Christ suffered death as men do, but as a priest he atoned for the sins of the world in a divine manner, and while there was an external shedding of blood there was also an internal and spiritual purgation, so that he died on earth but the virtue and efficacy of his death proceeded from heaven. On the words that follow Calvin reports that some render them, He could not be a priest of the number of those who offer gifts according to the Law, but prefers his own, He could not be a priest as long as there are priests who offer. On the copy and shadow he takes the verb to mean the performing of sacred rites, with a preposition to be understood, and judges this more appropriate than the rendering given by some, Who serve the shadow and example of heavenly things; in short, he teaches that the true worship of God consists not in the ceremonies of the Law, and that the Levitical priests while exercising their functions had nothing but a shadow and a copy inferior to the prototype. He thus anticipates a possible objection, showing that the worship of God according to the ancient sacrifices was not superfluous, because it referred to what was higher, even to heavenly realities.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson supply the argument and the words. Barnes calls the opening a general statement about the functions of the high priest: it was the peculiarity of the office, and constituted its essence, that some gift or sacrifice was to be presented, a priest being one who offers sacrifice mainly in behalf of others. The principles involved are that there is need of some offering or atonement for sin and a fitness that someone be designated to make it; and if a priest must offer sacrifice, then the name priest should not be given to anyone not appointed to offer sacrifice, and therefore not to the ministers of the gospel, since the great sacrifice for sin was once offered by the Lord Jesus and is not to be repeated. Accordingly, Barnes observes, the writers in the New Testament are perfectly uniform and consistent on this point, and the name priest is never once given to the ministers of the gospel. On the next verse he says the design is to show a reason why Christ was removed to heaven: on earth there were those already set apart to the office, and he, not being of the same tribe with them, could not officiate as priest, so that it was necessary that he should be removed to another sphere. On the copy and shadow he explains that they performed their service by the mere example and shadow of the heavenly things, in a tabernacle that was a mere copy of heaven; the word rendered example means a copy, likeness or imitation, the tabernacle having been made after a pattern shown to Moses so as to have some faint resemblance to the reality in heaven. A shadow, as of a man or a house or a tree, will indicate the form, the outline and the size of the object but has no substance or reality, and so it was with the rites of the Jewish religion, designed merely as a shadow of the substantial realities of the true religion. Ellicott explains that this verse and the three following confirm and illustrate the importance of the statement just made, the course of thought being that what stands at the head of what is being said, and gives completeness to the whole, is that we have a High Priest who ministers in heaven itself; for whereas the very conception of high-priestly duty would, were he on earth, exclude him from being a priest at all, like those who serve a copy of the heavenly things, he in heaven holds and exercises that more excellent ministry of which their service was a shadow and a type. He prefers the rendering that this High Priest also have somewhat to offer, and allows two senses: if the words refer to the continued ministration in the heavenly sanctuary the explanation is found later in the epistle, but the meaning may simply be that every high priest, and therefore the Lord Jesus, must have some sacrifice to present to God, this being the very object of his appointment. On the next verse he reports that the oldest Greek manuscripts and two important versions read, If then He were, and that two other changes in the text also rest on high authority, so that in its correct form the verse runs, If then He were on earth, He would not even be a priest, that is he would not be a priest at all, seeing there are those who according to law offer the gifts; the argument somewhat resembles that of the seventh chapter, but there the impediment is that of tribe, while here the thought is that the place is preoccupied by men who by express command are bringing the gifts unto God. On the copy and shadow Ellicott prefers, men who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, taking copy not in the sense of perfect resemblance but rather as a token suggesting and designed to suggest the original, and shadow as having no substance or independent existence but representing only the outline of an object; and he warns that we must not confound these words with the pattern mentioned in Exodus and quoted later in this verse. The heavenly things, he adds, are the sanctuary and the tabernacle of the earlier verses, the realities to which the true earthly tabernacle corresponded, and Moses was charged in all respects to follow the pattern which had been shown him in the mount, that every part of God's earthly house might be a fitting emblem of spiritual truth to be afterwards revealed. Robertson notes the articular infinitive of purpose in the opening, calls the necessity a moral and logical one, and observes that there is no word for high priest in the following clause. On the next verse he marks a condition of the second class, determined as unfulfilled, so that the sense is, not even would he be a priest, and adds that Jesus was not of the tribe of Levi and so could not serve here. On the copy and shadow he notes that the two datives form a practical hendiadys for a shadowy outline, that the verb rendered warned of God does not contain the word God though it is implied, and that the word rendered pattern is the very one used in Exodus and quoted by Stephen.

Clarke and Wesley take the offerings and the figure. Clarke glosses the opening verb as being set apart for this especial work, and distinguishes the two offerings: eucharistic offerings, by which God's government of the universe and his benevolence in providing for his creatures were acknowledged, and sacrifices for sin, by which the destructive and ruinous nature of sin and the necessity of an atonement were confessed. If Christ be a high priest, he argues, and it be essential to the office of a high priest to offer atoning sacrifices to God, Jesus must offer such; and it is manifest that as he is the public minister officiating in the true tabernacle he must make an atonement, while his being at the right hand of the throne shows that he has offered and continues to offer such an atonement. On the next verse Clarke observes that the Jewish temple was standing when this epistle was written, so that the whole temple service continued to be performed by the legal priests, descendants of Aaron of the tribe of Levi; therefore if Christ had been then on earth he could not have performed the office of a priest, being of the tribe of Judah, to which the priesthood did not appertain. This, he says, is an additional proof that the epistle was written before the destruction of Jerusalem; and he asks, since the word for sacrifices is not added here as in the previous verse, whether that is evidence that bloody sacrifices had then ceased to be offered, or whether both kinds are included in the word for gifts, doubting whether that word is ever used to express a bloody sacrifice and believing that the Septuagint never used it so. On the copy and shadow Clarke renders it, with the representation and shadow, which he takes from Macknight and thinks probably the true translation: the whole Levitical service was a representation and shadow of heavenly things, and it appears absurd to say that the priests served unto an example or representation of heavenly things, since they served rather unto the substance of those things, with appropriate representations and shadows. Moses, he notes, was divinely warned or admonished of God, and the pattern is the type, plan or form; it is very likely, he adds, that God gave a regular plan and specification of the tabernacle and all its parts to Moses, and that from this divine plan the whole was constructed. Wesley says that if Christ's priesthood terminated on earth he could not be a priest at all, consistently with the Jewish institutions, there being other priests to whom alone this office is allotted; that those who serve, serve the temple, which was not yet destroyed; and that the pattern and shadow are of spiritual, evangelical worship and of everlasting glory. The pattern he likens to the strokes pencilled out upon a piece of fine linen, which exhibit the figures of leaves and flowers but have not yet received their splendid colours and curious shades, and the shadow to a shadowy representation which gives some dim and imperfect idea of the body but not the fine features, not the distinguishing air, none of those living graces which adorn the real person; yet both the pattern and the shadow lead our minds to something nobler than themselves, the pattern to that holiness and glory which complete it, and the shadow to that which occasions it.

debates: What the necessity of a sacrifice proves. Calvin makes it the hinge of the whole argument, that a priesthood without a sacrifice is an empty name and Christ's therefore is not earthly; Barnes turns it into a rule about the word priest, denying the name to gospel ministers since the one sacrifice is not repeated; Clarke infers a continuing offering from the session at the right hand; Ellicott leaves the reference open between a continued heavenly ministration and the bare rule that every priest must have something to present.

Why he could not be a priest on earth. Barnes, Clarke and Robertson all make the impediment his tribe, since the office was already held by the sons of Levi; Ellicott expressly distinguishes his reading from that argument, holding on the older manuscripts that the impediment is rather that the place is preoccupied by men commanded to bring the gifts, and Wesley reads it the same way; Calvin prefers a rendering that makes the priesthood impossible only so long as those priests continue.

How the priests stand to the copy and shadow. Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson expound the two words as they stand, Ellicott warning that they must not be confounded with the pattern named later; Clarke and Calvin both reject the received construction, holding it absurd that the priests should serve unto a representation, and reading instead that they served with representations and shadows.

What the pattern in the mount implies. Clarke supposes a regular plan and specification given to Moses; Robertson identifies the word as the one used in Exodus and quoted by Stephen; Ellicott makes the charge one of exact conformity so that every part might be an emblem of truth later revealed; Calvin turns it into an answer to the objection that the old worship was superfluous.
outliers: Gill alone writes against a named party, answering the Socinian argument that this verse denies Christ any priesthood or sacrifice on earth by distinguishing the offering of himself, which was on earth, from the ministration that followed it in heaven.
Barnes alone draws a conclusion about Christian ministry from the definition of a priest, observing that the New Testament never once gives the name to a minister of the gospel.
themes: priests that offer gifts according to the law
the example and shadow of heavenly things
as Moses was admonished of God
according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount

6.pericope_label: But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, then should no place have been sought for the second.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the ministry and the covenant. Gill notes that Christ has a ministry, being the minister of the sanctuary, and that he obtained it of his Father, being called to it and engaged in it by him; though called to it from eternity, it was in time that he came a high priest of good things to come. On the first covenant Gill is careful to say which covenant is not meant. It is not the covenant of works: that was made in paradise while this was on Mount Sinai, that was made with Adam and his posterity while this was with the Jews only, that had no mediator while this had one in Moses, that was not dedicated with blood while this was, that had no forgiveness of sin in it while this had, and to be under that was no privilege while to be under this was, as to the Israelites, who on this account were preferable to all other nations. Nor is the pure covenant of grace as administered under the Gospel meant: for though that was first made, it is the second in administration; that includes the elect of God among the Gentiles while this includes only the Jews; that is made known to them whom God calls by his grace in time while this was made with good and bad; that was of pure grace while this required works in order to life and the enjoyment of its blessings; and that is an everlasting covenant while this is done away, so that the one is manifestly distinguished from the other. Calvin argues that as the excellency of the covenant had before been inferred from the dignity of the priesthood, so now Christ's priesthood is maintained to be more excellent than Aaron's because he is the interpreter and Mediator of a better covenant. Both were necessary, for the Jews were to be led away from the superstitious observance of rituals by which they were prevented from advancing directly to the real and pure truth of the Gospel; and it was but right that Moses and Aaron should give way to Christ as to one more excellent, because the gospel is a more excellent covenant than the Law and because the death of Christ was a nobler sacrifice than the victims under the Law. What is added, Calvin says, is not without some difficulty, that the covenant of the Gospel was proclaimed on better promises; and on the word he notes that the verb means what is set as a law, that is firmly and irrevocably fixed, so that it was a covenant firmly founded on more excellent promises, which the following verses specify. On the next verse he holds that the writer confirms what he had said of the excellency of the covenant on this ground, that the covenant of the Law was neither valid nor permanent, for if nothing was wanting in it why was another substituted for it? Since another has been substituted, it is evident that the old covenant was not in every respect perfect, and to prove this he adduces the testimony of Jeremiah. But it seems hardly consistent, Calvin objects, that after saying no place would have been sought for the second covenant had the first been faultless, he should then say that the people were at fault and that for this cause the new covenant was introduced as a remedy; it appears unjust that if the blame was in the people it should be transferred to God's covenant, and the argument seems not valid, for though God might a hundred times have blamed the people, the covenant could not on that account be deemed faulty. The answer, he says, may be easily given: though the crime of violating the covenant was justly imputed to the people, who had through their own perfidy departed from God, yet the weakness of the covenant is also pointed out, because it was not written where it would hold.

Henry illustrates the superior excellency of the priesthood of Christ above that of Aaron from the excellency of that dispensation of the covenant of grace of which Christ was the Mediator: his ministry is more excellent by how much he is the Mediator of a better covenant. The body and soul too of all divinity, as some observe, consist very much in rightly distinguishing between the two covenants, the covenant of works and the covenant of grace, and between the two dispensations of the covenant of grace, that under the Old Testament and that under the New. Of the old dispensation Henry says that it was made with the fathers of the Jewish nation at mount Sinai, and that Moses was the Mediator of that covenant, when God took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, which intimates the great affection, condescension and tender care of God towards them; and that this covenant was not found faultless, being a dispensation of darkness and dread, tending to bondage, and only a schoolmaster to bring us to Christ. He adds that the law not only made all subject to it liable to be condemned for the guilt of sin, but was also unable to remove that guilt and clear the conscience from the sense and terror of it, whereas by the blood of Christ a full remission of sins was provided, so that God would remember them no more.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle the comparison and the words. Barnes explains the more excellent ministry as a service of a higher order or of a more exalted nature, the real and substantial service of which the other was but the emblem, pertaining to things in heaven while the other was concerned with the earthly tabernacle, and enduring while that was to vanish away; by as much as the new covenant is more important than the old, by so much does his ministry exceed in dignity that under the ancient dispensation. Christ officiates between God and man according to the arrangements of the new covenant, and the word rendered covenant properly denotes a disposition, arrangement or ordering of things, being employed in Scripture to describe the arrangement God has made to secure the maintenance of his worship on earth and the salvation of men; it is uniformly used in the Greek Old Testament and in the New Testament to denote the covenant which God makes with men, while the word which properly denotes a covenant or compact is never used. On the next verse Barnes says it is implied that God had said that covenant was not perfect or faultless; the meaning is not that the first covenant made under Moses had any real faults, or inculcated what was wrong, but that it did not contain the ample provision for the pardon of sin and the salvation of the soul which was desirable, being merely preparatory to the gospel. Had it been faultless there could have been no place sought for a second, since it would then have been impossible to better it and any change would have been only for the worse. Ellicott calls this another of those proportional statements found earlier in the epistle, the closest being that by how much the Priest appointed by the divine oath is raised above all other priests, by so much is his covenant better than theirs; here, as he is Mediator of a better covenant, in the same proportion does his ministry excel that of priests on earth. He would render the next clause one that hath been ordained, noting that the verb properly means to legislate and has already occurred where the people are said to have received the Law, so that a word which properly refers to the passing of a law is applied to a covenant; the explanation must be sought in the special nature of the covenants of God with man, which are not compacts between equals but arrangements offered by the divine goodness and made dependent upon conditions, so that such a covenant may be spoken of as ordained or enacted on the basis of promise, the promises given by God being the basis of the covenant which becomes the law of his kingdom and the declaration of his procedure. On the next verse Ellicott would render it for a second rather than for the second, connecting the verse with the words a better covenant, and says the form of expression clearly points to the intended inference, that the covenant was faulty and a place was sought for a second; the failure of the first covenant was manifest to God, who, whilst the first still existed, sought and found place for a second. Robertson glosses the opening as the case now stands, with Jesus as high priest in heaven, notes the perfect of a rare and late verb meaning to hit the mark or attain, and says the remark about a more excellent ministry applies to all the five points of superiority over the Levitical priesthood. The word mediator he derives from the word for amid, so that it means a middle man or arbitrator; the covenant is called new elsewhere in the epistle; and the verb rendered established he renders hath been enacted, the promises being the basis on which it rests. But how, he asks, are the promises better if the earlier were also from God? On the next verse he notes that the word covenant is not expressed but is clearly meant by the feminine gender, that the adjective rendered faultless is an old compound, and that the condition is of the second class and assumes that the old covenant was not blameless, apparently a serious charge which the writer hastens to explain.

Clarke and Wesley measure the two covenants. Clarke says Christ's office of priesthood is more excellent than the Levitical because the covenant is better and established on better promises: the old covenant referred to earthly things and the new to heavenly, the old had promises of secular good and the new of spiritual and eternal blessings; and as far as Christianity is preferable to Judaism, as far as Christ is preferable to Moses, as far as spiritual blessings are preferable to earthly, and as far as the enjoyment of God throughout eternity is preferable to the communication of earthly good during time, so far does the new covenant exceed the old. On the next verse he says the argument is nearly the same as one used earlier: if the first covenant had made provision for and actually conferred pardon and purity, and given a title to eternal life, there could have been no need for a second; but the first covenant did not give these things, therefore a second was necessary, and the covenant that gives these things is the Christian covenant. Wesley says Christ's priesthood as much excels theirs as the promises of the gospel, whereof he is a surety, excel those of the law, and that these better promises are specified in the verses that follow, those in the law being mostly temporal promises. On the next verse he says that if that dispensation had answered all God's designs and man's wants, if it had not been weak and unprofitable and unable to make anything perfect, no place would have been for a second.

debates: What makes the promises better. Clarke sets earthly against heavenly and secular good against spiritual and eternal blessing; Wesley points forward to the verses that specify them and calls the promises of the law mostly temporal; Calvin and Robertson both stop at the difficulty, that it is not obvious how promises can be called better if the earlier ones were also from God.

What the verb rendered established means. Ellicott would render it ordained, since the word properly means to legislate, and explains the usage from the nature of God's covenants, which are not compacts between equals but arrangements offered on conditions; Robertson renders it enacted; Calvin fixes the sense as what is set as a law, firmly and irrevocably; Barnes makes the parallel point on the noun, that the ordinary Greek word for a compact between parties is never used.

What was faulty in the first covenant. Barnes denies that it had any real fault and locates the defect in what it lacked, ample provision for pardon; Clarke and Wesley argue from the mere fact of a second, since a covenant that conferred pardon and a title to life would have left no room for another; Ellicott says the failure was manifest to God, who sought place for a second while the first still stood; Robertson calls the charge a serious one which the writer hastens to explain; Calvin alone treats the whole as an objection to be answered.

Which covenant the first is. Gill alone stops to exclude two others: not the covenant of works, made in paradise with Adam, without mediator or forgiveness, whereas this was made at Sinai with the Jews through Moses and dedicated with blood; nor the covenant of grace as administered under the gospel, which though made first is second in administration, reaches the Gentiles, is of pure grace and is everlasting, whereas this required works and is done away.
outliers: Calvin alone frames the chapter's central move as an objection against itself, asking how blame that lies in the people can be transferred to God's covenant, and answering that both are true at once, since the people's perfidy and the covenant's weakness are pointed out together.

Gill alone spends his comment on saying which covenant is not meant, separating the first covenant here from the covenant of works on one side and from the covenant of grace as now administered on the other.
themes: the mediator of a better covenant
if that first covenant had been faultless
no place have been sought for the second

8.pericope_label: For finding fault with them, he saith, Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah: Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they continued not in my covenant, and I regarded them not, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the fault and the prophecy. Gill says the fault is found both with the covenant, which had its faults, and with the people, who continued not in it and were therefore disregarded by the Lord; and that the fathers with whom the covenant was made are the ancestors of the Jews at Mount Sinai. Calvin explains that the prophet speaks of future time and arraigns the people of perfidy, because they continued not faithful after having received the Law, so that the Law was the covenant which was broken, as God complains, by the people; to remedy this evil he promised a new and different covenant, the fulfilment of which prophecy was the abrogation of the old. But it may be said, Calvin objects, that the Apostle seems unreasonably to turn this prophecy to suit his own purpose, for here the question is respecting ceremonies while the Prophet speaks of the whole Law: what has it to do with ceremonies, when God inscribes on the heart the rule of a godly and holy life delivered by the voice and teaching of men? To this he replies that the argument is applied from the whole to a part, since there is no doubt that the Prophet includes the whole dispensation of Moses when he says, I have made with you a covenant which you have not kept; and besides, the Law was in a manner clothed with ceremonies, and when the body is dead what is the use of garments? It is a common saying that the accessory is of the same character as its principal, and no wonder then that the ceremonies, which are nothing more than appendages to the old covenant, should come to an end. On the next verse Calvin says the difference between the covenant which then existed and the new one is here expressed: the Prophet might have said only that he would renew the covenant which through their fault had come to nothing, but he expressly declares that it would be one unlike the former. By saying that the covenant was made in the day when he laid hold on their hand to rescue them from bondage, he enhanced the sin of defection by reminding them of so great a benefit; and he did not accuse one age only of ingratitude, but since these very men who had been delivered immediately fell away, and their posterity after their example continually relapsed, the whole nation had become covenant-breakers. By saying that he neglected them or cared not for them, Calvin adds, the Prophet intimates that it would profit them nothing to have been once adopted as his people unless he succoured them by this new kind of remedy; and he notes that the Prophet expresses in Hebrew something more, but that this has little to do with the present question.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson divide over the object of the complaint. Barnes reports two schools and adds a third reading. Some understand the sense to be that the fault is found not with the Jewish people, who had had nothing to do in giving the covenant, but with the covenant itself, so that God, stating its defects, had said to them that he would give them one more perfect of which that was only preparatory; so Stuart, Rosenmuller and Erasmus understand it. Doddridge, Koppe and many others understand it as it stands in the English translation, as implying that the fault was found with the people, and refer to the passage quoted from Jeremiah, where the complaint is of the people; and Barnes allows that the Greek may bear either construction. He then asks whether a somewhat different interpretation may not be adopted, that using language of complaint, or language which implied that there was defect or error, he speaks of another covenant; on this the idea would be that he found fault specifically neither with the covenant nor with the people, but generally used language implying that there was a defect somewhere when he promised another and a better covenant. The word rendered finding fault, Barnes notes, properly means to censure or to blame. On the next verse he explains that the arrangement made with the fathers related mainly to outward observances and temporal blessings, and that the new dispensation would differ from that made when they came out of Egypt, the respects being specified in the verses following; in Jeremiah the breach of the covenant is stated as a simple fact, while in the apostle's quotation it is given as a reason why God would give a new arrangement, the apostle having quoted literally from the Greek version without materially varying the sense. The word rendered because, he adds, may mean since, so that the sense is that since they did not obey that covenant, and it was ineffectual in keeping them from sin, showing that it was not perfect or complete in regard to what was needful for man, a new arrangement should be made without defect. Ellicott decides that the fault is found not with it but with those through whom the covenant had failed. He notes that the quotation is taken from Jeremiah, the crowning point of the collection of prophecies gathered in those chapters and descriptive of the hope and salvation of Israel; that it agrees in the main with the Greek version and in one clause only fails to represent the meaning of the Hebrew original; and that the only point requiring notice in this verse is the substitution of I will accomplish for I will make, the new word closely answering to the word rendered ordained earlier in the chapter. On the next verse he says that in the day when they were led forth out of Egypt the token of God's covenant was the deliverance itself, while at Sinai the book of the covenant was read and the blood of the covenant sprinkled on the people, who had promised obedience to all the words that the Lord had said. It is here, he adds, that the translation departs from the Hebrew, which as is now generally believed is faithfully represented in the Authorised version, although I was an husband unto them, that is, had the authority of a husband; the quotation here follows the Greek version without change. Robertson notes that the participle rendered finding fault is a present middle of an old verb occurring only here and in Romans, and states the case plainly: the covenant was all right, but the Jews failed to keep it, and hence God made a new one of grace in place of law. He observes that the writer quotes the passage in full because it calls for little explanation or application to prove his point, glosses the verb rendered I will make as an old compound meaning to accomplish, and distinguishes the word used here for new, which means fresh and on new lines as opposed to the old, from the other Greek word which means young or not yet old. On the next verse he calls the construction a Hellenistic innovation in imitation of the Hebrew, notes the technical genitive of the part affected in by the hand and the infinitive of purpose in to lead them forth, and says that the Israelites broke the covenant and God then annulled it, the word rendered I regarded not meaning I neglected, since the covenant was void when they broke it.

Clarke and Wesley take the promise and its extent. Clarke explains the meaning to be that God, in order to show that the first covenant was inefficient, says to the Israelites that the days come when he will make a new covenant: he found fault with the covenant and addressed the people concerning his purpose of giving another, such as the necessities of mankind required; and since the place refers to Jeremiah, the words finding fault with them may refer to the Jewish people, of whom the Lord complains that they had broken his covenant though he was a husband to them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah he takes to mean all the descendants of the twelve sons of Jacob, and reports that this is thought to be a promise of the conversion of all the Jews to Christianity, both of the lost tribes and of those known to exist in Asiatic and European countries. On the next verse he says the new covenant is of a widely different nature from the old, which was only temporal and earthly in itself though it pointed out spiritual and eternal things, and that the Jews should have been prepared to expect such a covenant since Jeremiah had so clearly foretold it. He observes that the word we translate covenant often means religion itself and its various precepts, and that the old covenant in general stated on God's side, I will be your God, and on the Israelites' side, We will be thy people, which covenant they brake by serving other gods and neglecting the precepts of that holy religion. On the closing clause Clarke notes that the Greek means I neglected them or despised them, while the words in the Hebrew text of the prophet are translated, although I was a husband to them; and he asks, if our translation be correct, how it is possible to account for this most strange difference between the apostle and the prophet, and whether the Spirit of God could be the author of such a strange, not to say contradictory, rendering. Wesley says that God, finding fault with those who were under the old covenant, makes a new covenant with the house of Israel, that is with all the Israel of God, in all ages and nations. It is new in many respects, he explains, though not as to the substance of it: being ratified by the death of Christ, freed from those burdensome rites and ceremonies, containing a more full and clear account of spiritual religion, attended with larger influences of the Spirit, extended to all men, and never to be abolished. On the next verse he glosses the taking by the hand as done with the care and tenderness of a parent, and observes that just while this was fresh in their memory they obeyed, but presently after they shook off the yoke, so that they continued not in the covenant and God regarded them not, that covenant being soon broken in pieces.

debates: With whom the fault is found. Barnes reports one school, naming Stuart, Rosenmuller and Erasmus, which finds it with the covenant, and another, naming Doddridge and Koppe, which finds it with the people, allows that the Greek bears either, and proposes a third sense in which neither is blamed specifically but language of complaint implies a defect somewhere; Ellicott and Robertson both decide for the people; Gill and Clarke take both together.

Whether the prophecy fits the argument. Calvin raises the objection himself, that the question here is of ceremonies while Jeremiah speaks of the whole Law, and answers that the argument runs from the whole to a part, the Law having been clothed with ceremonies which are mere appendages and must fall with it.

Who is promised the new covenant. Clarke takes the two houses for all the descendants of Jacob and reports the view that a conversion of all the Jews is promised, including the lost tribes; Wesley reads it of all the Israel of God in all ages and nations, and lists six respects in which the covenant is new though not new in substance.

How the departure from the Hebrew is to be met. Clarke is scandalised and asks how the Spirit of God could author what looks like a contradiction; Ellicott records calmly that the translation here departs from the Hebrew, which the English version faithfully represents, the quotation following the Greek version; Calvin observes that the Hebrew says something more and sets it aside as irrelevant to the question in hand; Robertson simply expounds the Greek.
outliers: Barnes alone sets out the interpreters by name on both sides before proposing a reading that would make the complaint general rather than aimed at either the covenant or the people.
Clarke alone treats the divergence between the apostle's quotation and the Hebrew text as a scandal requiring an account, where the others either explain it from the Greek version or pass it by.
themes: I took them by the hand
to lead them out of the land of Egypt
they continued not in my covenant

10.pericope_label: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, saith the Lord; I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts: and I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people: And they shall not teach every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the Lord: for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the covenant and its inward working. Gill explains that this is the sum and substance of the covenant which God promised to make manifest and known to his chosen people, the true Israelites, under the Gospel dispensation, the following being the several articles of it. On the promise about teaching he is careful to say what it does not mean: it is not to be understood so as to set aside the external and public ministry of the word, which is a standing ordinance of God under the Gospel dispensation, or even the private instructions of saints one to another, whereby they may build up one another in their most holy faith; the sense is that men should not only teach, but that the Spirit of God should teach with them and by them. It stands opposed, Gill adds, to particular and pretended revelations, and especially to magisterial dictates, and denotes the abundance of knowledge that should be in Gospel times, which should not be restrained to particular persons and sets of men but shared by all believers, more or less. Calvin finds two main parts in this covenant, the first the gratuitous remission of sins and the other the inward renovation of the heart, with a third which depends on the second, the illumination of the mind as to the knowledge of God. There are many things here deserving of notice, he says, the first being that God calls us to himself without effect as long as he speaks to us in no other way than by the voice of man: he teaches us and commands what is right, but he speaks to the deaf, for when we seem to hear anything our ears are only struck by an empty sound, and the heart, full of depravity and perverseness, rejects every wholesome doctrine. In short, the word of God never penetrates into our hearts, for they are iron and stone until they are softened by him; nay, they have engraven on them a contrary law, for perverse passions rule within which lead us to rebellion. In vain then does God proclaim his Law by the voice of man, unless he writes it by his Spirit on our hearts, that is, unless he forms and prepares us for obedience; and hence it appears, Calvin concludes, of what avail is freewill and the uprightness of nature before God regenerates us. On the next verse he says the third point is as it were a part of the second, since it is the work of the Spirit of God to illuminate our minds so that we may know what the will of God is, and also to bend our hearts to obedience; for the right knowledge of God is a wisdom which far surpasses the comprehension of man's understanding, and to attain it no one is able except through the secret revelation of the Spirit. Hence Isaiah, speaking of the restoration of the Church, says that all God's children would be his disciples, and the meaning of the Prophet here is the same; for God does not promise what is in our own power, but what he alone can perform for us, so that these words are the same as though he had said that our minds are blind and destitute of all right understanding until they are illuminated by the Spirit of God, and that God is rightly known by those alone to whom he has been pleased by a special favour to reveal himself. By the words from the least to the greatest he first intimates that God's grace would be poured on all ranks of men, so that no class would be without it.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson expound the promises. Barnes calls this the arrangement which shall succeed the old one, made with the true Israel, that is with all those whom God will regard and treat as his friends. The phrase after those days, he says, may either mean that after those days God will put his laws in their hearts or that he will make this covenant with them after those days, the difference being merely in the punctuation and the sense not materially affected; but it seems to him that the meaning of the Hebrew in Jeremiah is, in those after days, that is in the period called in Scripture the last days or the ages to come, meaning the last dispensation of the world, so that the promise belongs to the times of the Messiah. The laws put into the mind, he explains, would not be mere external observances but would affect the conscience and the heart, the laws of the Hebrews having pertained mainly to external rites and ceremonies while the laws of the new dispensation relate particularly to the inner man. On the next verse Barnes says that no one shall be under a necessity of imparting instruction to another or of exhorting him to become acquainted with the Lord, which sets forth another advantage of the new dispensation over the old; the knowledge of the Lord and of the true religion would be deeply engraved on the minds of all, so that there would be no necessity for mutual exhortation and counsel, and he quotes Doddridge that they shall have a much more certain and effectual teaching than they can derive from another. The passage, Barnes warns, does not refer to the fact that the true religion will be universally diffused, but to the accurate and just knowledge of the Lord among those who are interested in the blessings of the new covenant, who would be so taught respecting his character that they would not need the aid to be derived from others. Ellicott renders the opening verb literally as I will covenant, noting that it is not the same word as in the earlier verse, and observes that where formerly the prophecy named Israel and Judah, the reunion of the nation having once been signified, Israel could stand alone as the name of the one people. He would render the next clause, putting my laws into their mind, I will also write them on their heart, noting that in the former clause the Hebrew has, I will put my law in their inward parts, so that the law shall be within them and not an external code, while in the latter the fleshy tablets of the heart are contrasted with the tables of the Law; this, he says, is the first of the better promises. On the next verse he prefers fellow-citizen to neighbour according to the best reading, and calls the second promise the universality of the knowledge of God, the divine teaching being not only internal but for this very reason extending to all. Robertson notes the future middle of the cognate verb, that I will covenant, and the present participle rendered I will put; the mind is the intellect, the moral understanding, and the heart is the seat of man's personal life, the two terms covering the whole of man's inward nature. He observes the Hebraistic construction in the clauses about being a God and a people, and remarks that this was the ideal of the old covenant, now at last to be a fact. On the next verse he notes the strong double negative with the aorist subjunctive, prefers his fellow-citizen, and says that in the new covenant all will be taught of God, whereas under the old only the educated scribe could understand the minutiae of the law; the verb rendered shall know is one of the rare future perfects.

Clarke and Wesley take the inward law and the public teaching. Clarke calls this the nature of that glorious system of religion which God will publish in the times of the Gospel: he will influence them with the principles of law, truth and holiness, and their understandings shall be fully enlightened to comprehend them, while all their affections, passions and appetites shall be purified and filled with holiness and love to God and man, so that they shall willingly obey and feel that love is the fulfilling of the law; instead of being written on tables of stone, the laws shall be written on the fleshly tables of their hearts. He calls the two clauses that follow the two grand conditions by which the parties in this covenant are bound, that God will be their God and they shall be his people; as the object of religious adoration is that Being from whom a man expects light, direction, defence, support and happiness, God in promising to be their God promises in effect to give them all these great and good things, while to be God's people implies that they should give God their whole hearts and serve him with all their light and strength, having no other object of worship. On the next verse Clarke argues from the state of things under the old covenant, where properly speaking there was no public instruction: before the erection of synagogues all worship was confined at first to the tabernacle and afterwards to the temple, and when synagogues were established they were used principally for the bare reading of the law and the prophets, so that scarcely any such thing as a public ministry for the continual instruction of the common people was found in the land till the time of John the Baptist, our Lord and his apostles. There were prophets who were a sort of general teachers, but neither was their ministry extended through all the people, and there were schools of the prophets and schools of the rabbins, but these were for the instruction of select persons; hence it was necessary that every man should do what he could, under that dispensation, to instruct his neighbour and brother. The prophecy, Clarke says, indicates that there should be under the Gospel dispensation a profusion of divine light, which we find to be the case by the plentiful diffusion of the sacred writings and by an abundant Gospel ministry, blessings not confined to temples or palaces but found in every corner of the land. Wesley dates the covenant from the abolition of the Mosaic dispensation, and explains that God will open their eyes and enlighten their understanding to see the true, full, spiritual meaning of his laws, and write them on their hearts so that they shall inwardly experience whatever he has commanded; that he will be to them a God, their all-sufficient portion and exceeding great reward, and they shall be to him a people, his treasure and his beloved, loving and obedient children. On the next verse he grants that in other respects those under this covenant will have need to teach each other to their lives' end, but says they shall not need to teach every one his brother saying, Know the Lord, for all real Christians shall know him. On the order of the words he observes that in this order the saving knowledge of God ever did and ever will proceed, not first to the greatest and then to the least, citing the promise that the Lord shall save the tents of Judah first, that the glory of the house of David and of the inhabitants of Jerusalem do not magnify themselves.

debates: Who the house of Israel now is. Gill and Barnes both read it spiritually, of the chosen people or of all whom God treats as his friends; Ellicott explains the single name historically, that once the reunion of the nation had been signified Israel could stand for the whole people.

What the writing on the heart effects. Ellicott, Barnes and Robertson expound the contrast between an external code and the inward nature, Robertson adding that this was already the ideal of the old covenant; Clarke and Wesley describe the enlightening of the understanding and the purifying of the affections; Calvin alone turns the promise into an argument about the will, holding that the word never penetrates hearts of iron and stone until God softens them, and drawing the conclusion that freewill and the uprightness of nature avail nothing before regeneration.

What the promise about teaching abolishes. Clarke answers from institutions, that there was almost no public instruction under the old covenant and a profusion of light under the new; Gill denies that either the public ministry or private mutual instruction is set aside, and reads the promise against pretended revelations and magisterial dictates; Barnes takes it of necessity rather than practice and warns that universal diffusion of religion is not in view; Robertson makes the contrast one of learning, since only the trained scribe could master the law; Wesley concedes that in other respects Christians must teach each other to the end of life.

What the order from the least to the greatest signifies. Calvin takes it of rank, that grace would be poured on all classes without exception; Wesley insists on the sequence itself, that saving knowledge proceeds to the least first and never to the greatest first, and supports it from the promise about the tents of Judah.
outliers: Calvin alone makes the verse a proof text about the will, arguing from the necessity of the inward writing that human freewill and natural uprightness are worth nothing before God regenerates us.

Clarke alone answers the promise about teaching by a survey of Jewish institutions, arguing that public instruction of the common people scarcely existed before John the Baptist, so that the mutual teaching the prophecy sets aside was a necessity of that dispensation.
themes: I will put my laws into their mind
I will be to them a God
they shall be to me a people
they shall not teach every man his neighbour
from the least to the greatest

12.pericope_label: For I will be merciful to their unrighteousness, and their sins and their iniquities will I remember no more. In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the pardon and the abrogation. Gill explains that the unrighteousness is sin, since all unrighteousness is sin, being contrary to the justice of God and his righteous law, and that the phrase expresses God's forgiveness of it, a very considerable article of the covenant of grace. Mercy is the spring and original of pardon; it is what God delights in, and therefore he pardons freely; it is large and abundant, and hence he pardons fully, which lays a foundation for hope in sensible sinners. The way and means by which God pardons is the propitiatory sacrifice of his Son, and the word here rendered merciful signifies propitious: God pardons none but those to whom he is pacified, or rendered propitious, by Christ, and there is no mercy nor pardon but through him, since he pardons on the foot of reconciliation and satisfaction for sin by Christ, so that forgiveness of sin is an act of justice as well as of mercy, or an act of mercy streaming through the blood and sacrifice of Christ. On the last verse Gill notes only that the new covenant is meant of the prophecy just quoted. Calvin infers from the fact of one covenant being established the subversion of the other, and holds that by calling it the old covenant the writer assumes that it was to be abrogated, since what is old tends to a decay. The verse may be rendered, he says, by saying, a new covenant, he has made ancient the first; now what is ancient and becomes old is nigh a dissolution or disappearing. It is said to be ancient in contrast with the new, and old or aged is afterwards added in order to show its weak and feeble character, being like an old man tottering on the brink of the grave, who, when buried, disappears from among the living. It is supposed, Calvin adds, that there is here an intimation of the dissolution of the whole Jewish polity, which soon afterwards took place; and besides, as the new is substituted, the former must have come to an end, for the second is of another character. But if the whole dispensation of Moses, as far as it was opposed to the dispensation of Christ, has passed away, then the ceremonies also must have ceased.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson number the promise and weigh the words. Barnes says the blessing of pardon will be much more richly enjoyed under the new dispensation than under the old, and calls this the fourth circumstance adduced in which the new covenant surpasses the old. The old was comparatively severe in its inflictions, marked every offence with strictness, and employed the language of mercy much less frequently than that of justice, being a system where law and justice reigned rather than mercy; it is true that it contemplated pardon and made arrangements for it, but this is much more prominent in the new dispensation, where it is the leading idea which separates it from all other systems. The entire arrangement is one for the pardon of sin in a manner consistent with the claims of law and justice, bestowing forgiveness in the most ample and perfect manner on all who are interested in the plan; and the peculiarity by which the gospel is distinguished from all other systems, ancient and modern, philosophic and moral, pagan and deistical, is that it makes provision for the forgiveness of sin and actually bestows pardon on the guilty, which Barnes calls the centre, the crown and the glory of the new dispensation. On the last verse he explains that the use of the word new implies that the one it was to supersede was old, new and old standing in contradistinction from each other as we speak of a new and an old house or garment; the object is to show that by the very fact of an arrangement for a new dispensation differing so much from the old it was implied that the old was to be superseded and would vanish away. That which decays and waxes old is ready to vanish away is a general truth, which Barnes illustrates: an old house or garment, an ancient tree, an aged man, all have indications that they are soon to disappear, and the very fact of growing old is an indication that they will soon be gone; so the dispensation represented as old had symptoms of decay, having lost the vigour it had when fresh and new. Ellicott renders the first word literally as propitious, and would render the clause to their unrighteousnesses, and their sins will I remember no more, noting that the words rendered and their iniquities are omitted by the best authorities. Here, he says, is given the third and chief promise, the characteristic of the new covenant being the full pardon of sin; of this new covenant, ordained on the three promises of an inward revelation, universal knowledge of God, and free pardon of sin, Jesus is the Mediator. All these promises are present, virtually or formally, in the last portion of the argument, and in part they belong to the new covenant from the beginning; the pardon is spoken of not as a gift to individuals but rather as from the first a characteristic of the covenant. The first promise is seen in the gift of the Holy Spirit and in the teaching represented by the Sermon on the Mount, in which inward principles of life take the place of many an outward rule, while the second waits for full accomplishment but is seen in the abolition of distinctions between nation and nation and the common influence of the Holy Spirit; the subject has presented difficulties, Ellicott adds, because it has been forgotten that this Scripture speaks of no sudden change in man's relation to God. Robertson notes that the word rendered merciful is an old Attic adjective common in the Greek Old Testament and occurring only here in the New Testament, from which the verb for making propitiation comes, and that the promise to remember no more is a double negative with the aorist passive subjunctive. On the last verse he glosses the phrase as in the saying as to him, and takes the perfect of the verb rendered made old as meaning to treat as old and out of date, calling the conclusion much to the point. The second participle, he notes, comes from an old verb referring to the decay of old age, so that both ideas appear here in opposition to the two words for new; and the word rendered vanishing away is a late one for disappearance found only here in the New Testament. The author, Robertson concludes, writes as if the Old Testament legal and ceremonial system were about to vanish before the new covenant of grace, and asks whether, if he had written after the year seventy, he would not have written that it had vanished away.

Clarke and Wesley take the pardon and the date. Clarke observes that in order to be their God it is requisite that their iniquity should be pardoned, which is provided for by the immolation of Jesus Christ as the covenant sacrifice; by his blood redemption has been purchased, and all who with penitent hearts believe on the Lord Jesus receive remission of sins, God remembering their iniquities no more against them so as to punish them on that account. He then sets out the three terms under which all spiritual evil against the nature and law of God is here represented: unrighteousness, that is injustice or wrong, which is against God, one's neighbour and oneself; sin, that is deviation from the divine law, missing the mark, aiming at happiness but never attaining it because it is sought out of God and in the breach of his laws; and iniquity, that is lawlessness, not having, knowing or acknowledging a law, having no law written in the heart and being restrained by none in the conduct of life. All these are to be removed by God's mercy, and this is to be understood of his mercy in Christ Jesus. On the last verse Clarke says the first covenant has been considered as antiquated and no longer of any force, and finds in the words an allusion to the ancient laws which either had perished from the tables on which they were written through old age, or had fallen into disuse, or were abrogated; the phrase means it is about to be abolished, and he cites Dionysius of Halicarnassus, who says of the laws of Numa, written on oak boards, that they had perished through old age, the same Greek word being used to express the abolition of a law. The apostle therefore intimates that the old covenant was just about to be abolished, but expresses himself cautiously and tenderly, that he might not give unnecessary offence. Clarke adds that when the apostle said all shall know the Lord, from the least to the greatest, under the new covenant, he had copious authority for saying so from the rabbins themselves, citing a saying that in the days of the Messiah knowledge shall be renewed in the world and the law shall be made plain among all. Wesley reads the promise of mercy as meaning, I will justify them, which is the root of all true knowledge of God; this, he says, is God's method, that first a sinner is pardoned, then he knows God as gracious and merciful, then God's laws are written on his heart, so that he is God's and God is his. On the last verse he says that in saying a new covenant the writer has antiquated the first, showing that it is disannulled and out of date, and that what is antiquated is ready to vanish away, as it did quickly after, when the temple was destroyed.

debates: Where the promise of pardon stands in the series. Ellicott calls it the third and chief promise and makes the whole covenant rest on three; Barnes counts it the fourth of the advantages the new covenant has over the old; Wesley reverses the textual order into an order of experience, making justification the root of the knowledge of God and putting pardon first.

What the words governed by mercy are. Clarke expounds three terms as a graded account of evil, unrighteousness as injustice, sin as missing the mark, and iniquity as lawlessness; Ellicott reports that the best authorities omit the words about iniquities altogether and renders the clause of unrighteousnesses and sins alone; Gill and Robertson keep to the first word, which all three agree means propitious.

Whether the pardon is a gift or a property of the covenant. Ellicott insists that it is spoken of not as a gift to individuals but as from the first a characteristic of the covenant, and warns that difficulties have arisen from forgetting that no sudden change in man's relation to God is in view; Barnes describes it as an arrangement for pardon consistent with law and justice, bestowed on all who are interested in the plan.

How near the vanishing was. Clarke says the apostle intimates an abolition just at hand but writes cautiously to avoid offence; Wesley and Calvin both point to the destruction of the temple and the dissolution of the Jewish polity soon after; Robertson turns the tense into evidence for the date, asking whether a writer after the year seventy would not have said that the old system had vanished.
outliers: Robertson alone draws a conclusion about when the epistle was written from the tense of a single participle, arguing that a writer after the fall of Jerusalem would have spoken of a system already gone.
Clarke alone supports the promise of universal knowledge from rabbinic literature, citing a saying that in the days of the Messiah knowledge shall be renewed and the law made plain among all.
